title: What Holds a Civilisation Together: The Week in One Page
why: A week in five editions, and they turn out to circle the same question: what holds a civilisation together? Monday opened with Lee Harris taking on the citizen of the world, the cosmopolitan.
text:
A week in five editions, and they turn out to circle the same question: what holds a civilisation together? Monday opened with Lee Harris taking on the citizen of the world, the cosmopolitan. He traced the idea back to the Greek Diogenes, who called himself a citizen of the world simply because there is never any danger that such an abstract entity will make a concrete demand on him. A charming phrase, Harris shows, with a chilling skeleton underneath: the world asks nothing from you, and you owe it nothing in return. His closing turn was the gentlest line of the week. He suggests that patriotism is the indispensable prerequisite of a higher and more universal view, and he writes that the world is a vastly better place because it contains people whose only fault is the desire to make all people as good and reasonable as they themselves are.

Tuesday gave us Thucydides and the Melian Dialogue, the summer of 416 BC, when the great Athenian empire sent at least 3,400 men and 38 ships to the tiny island of Melos. The small city had stayed neutral in the long war, and Athens gave it the choice of tribute or destruction, with no moral argument at all. The strongest do what they can, the weak suffer what they must. What made the scene unforgettable was not just the lesson, but the choice of the man who wrote it: a historian of Athens let his own city be heard at its most brutal, without a single softening word.

Wednesday was Eric Hoffer, who argued that mass movements are far more alike than they look, even enemies. It is not the ideas that move people so much as the feeling of belonging and purpose a movement offers, the chance to fold your separate self into something bigger. His most memorable example was Saul, the fierce persecutor of the early Christians, who became Paul, their fiercest preacher. The man hardly changed, Hoffer says, the hunger did.

Thursday looked under the hood at how we judge: moral foundations theory, the idea that morality rests on a small set of instincts, care and fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity, and liberty. The famous finding is that the political camps feel so far apart because members of one are, to a degree, blind to one or more of the moral foundations of the others. The proposed remedy was charmingly concrete: walk around with all the foundations switched on, and the people on the far side of the wall stop looking like villains and start looking like neighbours with different priorities.

Friday closed the week with Harris on common sense. A team of psychologists at Cornell worried that most voters cannot tell a brilliant idea from a bad one. Harris had two answers. Extraordinarily clever people have held extraordinarily dumb ideas, so intelligence is no protection. And the best hope for democracy still lies in the unregulated marketplace of ideas, with the old caution: let the buyer beware. What connected the five editions is that no single thing saves a civilisation. Not the cosmopolitan ideal, not the strong, not the movement's devotion, not even moral instinct by itself. What kept recurring was the ordinary: belonging to places and people, patriotism as the floor rather than the ceiling of a wider outlook, listening past the blind spots built into every camp, and a homespun common sense that does not pretend the question is easy. If one line of the week is the most worth carrying, it is Harris's closing one, about a world made vastly better by people whose only fault is the desire to make all people as good and reasonable as they themselves are. Thucydides was the week's counterweight, and it worked. Athens made no moral case at all in the Melian Dialogue, and the point of the scene is to let us see what a world looks like when belonging, patriotism and common sense are removed from the equation, and only the strong are left. The rest of the week is, gently, the answer to what he records: not that such a world can be avoided, but that it is worth resisting, one community, one conversation, one switched on instinct at a time. Of the five threads, which one fits your own week most: a belonging that shaped you, a strong moment you had to resist, a hunger to belong you noticed, a blind spot you found in a quarrel, or a common sense you trusted against an expert? What would it take, next week, to tend that one thread a little more carefully?

title: The Common Sense That Saves Democracy
book: Are Americans Too Dumb for Democracy?
author: Lee Harris
why: In this essay Lee Harris takes on a fashionable complaint: that the ordinary voter is simply too unlearned to run a democracy, and that we would be better off leaving the hard choices to the experts.
text:
In this essay Lee Harris takes on a fashionable complaint: that the ordinary voter is simply too unlearned to run a democracy, and that we would be better off leaving the hard choices to the experts. The argument comes from a team of psychologists at Cornell, who worry that most of us cannot tell a brilliant idea from a bad one. Harris thinks this gets the picture exactly backwards, and he has two moves.

His first is historical. Extraordinarily clever people have held extraordinarily dumb ideas: George Bernard Shaw, Sidney and Beatrice Webb, Thorstein Veblen and Jawaharlal Nehru all thought Stalin's Soviet Union was a genuine worker's paradise. So a high IQ is no protection against a bad idea. And when Harris asks what the men who voted for Andrew Jackson in 1828 could tell you about Einstein, Darwin, Keynes or the internet, the answer is nothing, because none of those things had come to pass yet. And still, as he points out, if the unintelligent were ever going to do democracy in, they would have done it long ago. The real danger the old elites feared was never the foolish mob, but the demagogue, a charismatic figure who seizes power by playing on people's ignorance, like the dictators of Greece and Rome. America's outstanding record, Harris argues, is its refusal to hand too much power to any single person, and the credit belongs to what he calls the "homespun pragmatism of ordinary Americans, familiarly known as common sense."

His second move is aimed at the modern expert. The wise men of the Greek world could recognise one another, but today's brilliant neurologist, whom Harris dubs Frank, knows nothing at all about economics. And when we face a question that is too hard, we do exactly what Daniel Kahneman describes: we quietly substitute an easier question for it. We ask whether a doctor is prestigious instead of whether the treatment works, in the lovely way Harris's mother asked "Did you like him?" rather than "Is he a good doctor?" The upshot is not that we should stop trusting anyone, but that the best hope for democracy still lies in the "unregulated marketplace of ideas", with the old caution that "Let the buyer beware." This sits in a long argument that has run through Western thought since the Greeks, who thought the common people, the demos, were neither dispassionate enough nor clever enough to govern themselves. Harris is gently answering that classical case for rule by the elite, and his faith in common sense stands comfortably beside Tocqueville's trust in the self-governing wisdom of ordinary Americans. What makes the essay worth keeping is the humility it asks of both sides: we are cleverer than the experts suppose, and yet the world is complicated enough that no intelligence, however great, can take that complication away. Alexis de Tocqueville, who watched the young American democracy in the 1830s, looked at the same question from the other end. He was less afraid that the people were too stupid than that they were too much on their own, and that a majority left to itself could harden into a soft, paternal despotism that manages even willing adults for them. Harris is alert to the arrogance of the expert; Tocqueville is alert to the quiet power of the majority. Put together, the two suggest that a healthy democracy needs both a humble elite and citizens who stay tied to one another. Next time a confident expert or a headline tells you what to think, can you notice the easier question you are answering in place of the harder, real one? What would it feel like to sit with the harder one for a while, without hurrying to a tidy answer?

title: Six Instincts Behind Every Argument
author: Jonathan Haidt, Craig Joseph, and colleagues
why: Moral foundations theory, proposed in 2004 by the psychologists Jonathan Haidt and Craig Joseph and later expanded with colleagues, suggests that morality is not one thing, but rests on a small set of innate, modular foundations.
text:
Moral foundations theory, proposed in 2004 by the psychologists Jonathan Haidt and Craig Joseph and later expanded with colleagues, suggests that morality is not one thing, but rests on a small set of innate, modular foundations. What began as five grew to six: care and harm, fairness and cheating, loyalty and betrayal, authority and subversion, sanctity and degradation, and liberty and oppression. Haidt and his colleagues describe care and fairness as an 'individualizing cluster', and loyalty, authority and sanctity as a 'group-focused binding cluster'.

The theory grew out of what Haidt called moral dumbfounding: the experience of feeling that an act is wrong while being unable to say why. For Haidt, these moments support the idea that emotion drives moral judgement. In his formulation, moral judgement is 'caused by quick moral intuitions', and the reasoning we offer afterwards is largely a rationalization of a judgement that was already made.

The application that made the theory famous concerns politics. Measured with the Moral Foundations Questionnaire, progressives are most sensitive to care and fairness, conservatives to all the foundations, and libertarians to liberty, and Haidt and his colleagues suggest this is why the camps feel so far apart: members of one camp are 'to a degree, blind to one or more of the moral foundations of the others'. The proposed remedy is charmingly concrete. Picture politics as a wall, with the foundations as doorways, and spend some time walking around with all five switched on, and the people on the far side of the wall stop looking like villains and start looking like neighbours with different priorities. This idea sits in the conversation Lee Harris kept for much of his career about what groups do to the minds of their members: why loyalty to one's own tribe feels less like a preference than a moral duty. Moral foundations names that loyalty and shows how it binds, with the binding foundations of loyalty, authority and sanctity uniting a group against the wider world, while the individualizing foundations of care and fairness check the impulse from inside. It also deepens the elephant and rider picture from The Righteous Mind, where the elephant is the quick moral intuition and the rider the explanation we offer afterwards. It is worth carrying around today because it suggests that a great deal of what looks like stubbornness is two people caring about different, genuine moral things. The anthropologist Richard Shweder, whose work inspired Haidt, approached the same question from the other end. Rather than asking which moral feelings are innate, he asked what different cultures build with them, and found that societies organise their moral life around 'three distinct but coherent clusters of moral concerns': the ethics of autonomy, community and divinity. Shweder supplied the cultural map and Haidt the psychology, and the two agree on the most useful point of all: morality is plural and deeply felt, and understanding a community often starts with noticing which foundations it takes most seriously. The next time a disagreement feels stuck, try a small experiment: before answering, name the moral foundation the other person is speaking from. Is the argument really about the same thing, or are two different foundations talking past each other?

title: The Hunger to Belong: Hoffer on Mass Movements
book: The True Believer: Thoughts on the Nature of Mass Movements
author: Eric Hoffer
why: Eric Hoffer's big, humane claim is that mass movements are far more alike than they look.
text:
Eric Hoffer's big, humane claim is that mass movements are far more alike than they look. Communism and fascism were bitter enemies, yet he argues they are "interchangeable" in a very telling sense: they draw on the same deep human feeling, and they recruit the same kind of people. It is not really the ideas that move people, Hoffer says, but the feeling of belonging and purpose a movement offers, the chance to fold your separate self into something bigger and feel worthwhile at last.

He is gentle and specific about who is drawn in. The most likely recruits, he says, are the "New Poor", people who have fallen from comfort and now blame others for their fortunes, and the "misfits", those who feel their private life is meaningless and worthless. In every case the underlying experience is the same: a life that feels "irredeemably spoiled". A movement's chief work, he observes, is to "foster, perfect and perpetuate a facility for united action and self-sacrifice".

His most memorable example is Saul, the fierce persecutor of the early Christians, who became Paul, their fiercest preacher. The man hardly changed; the hunger did. And the most unsettling part of the picture is the need for an enemy. Without a "devil" to hate, a movement often wilts, because it is hatred that actually welds the believers together. Hoffer sits squarely in the orbit Lee Harris has been helping us read. Harris's central worry in Civilisation and Its Enemies is that modern society is being undermined by movements built on myth and resentment rather than reason, and Hoffer is one of the best thinkers for showing how that happens. The idea is worth carrying because it answers a smug assumption we often make, that fervour is always about ideas. It teaches us that much of what moves people is the hunger to belong, which is why a movement is understood through its feeling, not just its slogans. Alexis de Tocqueville saw the same human hunger from a different end, in the 1830s. Travelling through the young United States, he argued that modern democracy, with its equal and restless crowds, makes people feel small and gives them a longing for a strong, simple cause or leader. His worry was that this restlessness could lead people to surrender freedom willingly, because independence is tiring and asks for effort. Read together, he and Hoffer point at the same need, the desire to belong to something bigger, which civilisation handles better the more it learns to give that need good, gentle channels. Hoffer's lasting gift is to notice that much of our political heat is a hunger to belong rather than to believe. So, gently: where do you find your own sense of belonging, and is it something you are part of, or something you serve?

title: What the Strong Do: Thucydides on Power and Justice
author: Thucydides
why: In the summer of 416 BC, the great Athenian empire sent at least 3,400 men and 38 ships to a small island in the Aegean called Melos.
text:
In the summer of 416 BC, the great Athenian empire sent at least 3,400 men and 38 ships to a small island in the Aegean called Melos. The Melians were Dorians, the same people as the Spartans, and they had stayed neutral in the long war between Athens and Sparta. Athens demanded that they join the Delian League, the alliance of cities led by Athens, and pay tribute, or be destroyed. They refused. Thucydides, who was in exile at the time, did not witness the negotiations before the siege, but he wrote them up as a dialogue, and it has become one of the most talked about scenes in the whole of Greek history.

What makes the scene unforgettable is that the Athenians offer no moral justification at all. Their position is stated plainly: "the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must." The Melians then give the case for the weak, and it is moving. They are a neutral city, not an enemy. An invasion would alarm the other neutral states. It would be shameful to submit without a fight. The gods will help them because their cause is just, and their kinsmen in Sparta may come to their rescue. To each hope the Athenians reply, calmly and almost persuasively. Sparta has too little at stake to intervene. The other Greek cities will not fight for a distant island. The gods, they say, side with the strong, because that is the natural order of things. And hope itself, they add, is a luxury: if Melos resists it will probably lose, and come to bitterly regret what the text calls their irrational optimism.

The Melians did not submit. Athens blockaded the city until the following winter, and the hunger was so extreme that "Melian famine" entered the Greek language as a word for desperate starvation. When Melos finally fell, the Athenians executed the men of fighting age and sold the women and children into slavery. Thucydides says the point of the conquest was to show the strength and sternness of Athens, and to discourage the cities of the empire from rebelling. It did not work: a few years later, after the disastrous expedition to Sicily, rebellions broke out all across the empire, and the massacre had shocked the Greek world, even in Athens. The lasting gift of the dialogue, then, is not only its lesson about power. It is the choice of the man who wrote it. A historian of Athens let his own city be heard at its most brutal, without a single softening word, so that anyone who reads it, in any age, can judge the question for themselves. Thucydides wrote his History as the war was drawing to its close, and in the same work he gave us Pericles' funeral oration, a portrait of Athens at its ideal, shining and self confident. The two stand together on purpose: the best image a city has of itself, and the worst thing it did, both preserved without flattery. That is the permanent question at the heart of civilisation and its enemies. A civilisation that defends itself on raw power alone, and takes power to be all there is, fears everything on the outside while weakening itself on the inside. More than two thousand years later, whenever a person or a state has to decide what to do when it is stronger than the other side, this is still the first scene worth remembering. Plato staged the same question very differently. In the first book of the Republic, a sharp tongue called Thrasymachus insists that justice is nothing but the advantage of the stronger, which is close to the line Thucydides puts in the mouth of the Athenian envoys. Socrates' long answer is that justice is worth its cost, even for the person who practises it. Plato and Thucydides, the two great writers of Athens, agree that the question cannot be dodged. Plato holds it in a room, Thucydides holds it in a city under siege. Plato offers an answer; Thucydides leaves the question hanging in the air, which is probably why his scene still has its force. Where in your week do you hold the advantage, in a meeting, a family, a friendship? What would it look like, and what would it cost you, to act for the other person in that room rather than against them?

title: The Citizen of Nowhere: Harris on Patriotism and the World
book: The Cosmopolitan Illusion: The citizen of the world is a citizen of nowhere
author: Lee Harris
why: Harris takes on one of the most debated questions in education: should we teach our children to be patriotic, or to be citizens of the world before all else? His answer is not a flat refusal.
text:
Harris takes on one of the most debated questions in education: should we teach our children to be patriotic, or to be citizens of the world before all else? His answer is not a flat refusal. It is a careful excavation of what the cosmopolitan ideal actually is, and where it can quietly lead. The strongest form of the case, he grants, is that nationality is an accident, while being human is not. We may accidentally be Swiss or Indian, but we are essentially and necessarily human beings, and that is the one group no one can challenge as arbitrary.

He then traces the word to its origin with a lovely twist. When the Greek Diogenes was asked which city he had been brought up in, he answered that he was a "citizen of the world". Harris shows that this was not a tender universalism but the flip side of cynicism. The cynics modelled their lives on dogs, needing little and owing nothing to any city. Diogenes, Harris writes, consents to be a citizen only of a community that never exists, "simply because there is never any danger that such an abstract entity will make a concrete demand on him. The world asks nothing from him; he owes it nothing in return." A charming phrase, he suggests, with a chilling skeleton underneath.

His most original move is what he calls structural antagonism. Imagine two people with exactly the same aims and values, each fully aware that the other shares them. Could they not be at each other's throats? Obviously they could: two people who want the same woman, or the same piece of land. Conflict can arise precisely because the parties recognise one another, not because they fail to. Harris's closing turn is generous rather than gloomy: it may be that patriotism is the indispensable prerequisite of building a higher and more universal perspective, and the real question is not patriotism or cosmopolitanism, but what kind of each. And it is worth ending where he does. The world is a vastly better place, he writes, because it contains people "whose only fault is the desire to make all people as good and reasonable as they themselves are". The essay is a thread running through a great deal of Western thought. Harris borrows the Stoic image of concentric circles of loyalty from Nussbaum's essay, identifies Rawls's "veil of ignorance" as the real foundation of her position, and takes his closing insight on the Abbé de St. Pierre from Rousseau, who wrote of a man who "labored for imaginary beings, while believing that he was working for his contemporaries". His warning is one worth carrying into the present. The moment a universal vision is instantiated in a specific policy or curriculum, it loses its claim to represent what is universally desired and becomes just another agenda. Any ideal, however cosmopolitan, can become a particularism when the time comes to defend it with other people's children. Nussbaum herself offers the gentler image of the concentric circles, the self, then family, then the local community, then countrymen, with humanity as a whole outside all of them. Her aim is not to sever local loves but to train the student to "recognize humanity wherever she encounters it", undeterred by anything strange. Harris's complement is the reminder that mutual recognition is not a mechanism for resolving conflict, and that loyalty must eventually settle somewhere. What the two share is a shared refusal of narrowness: each wants education to enlarge the reader's circle of concern. What differs is whether the widest circle is a place you live, or a standard by which all smaller circles are judged. Think of the communities you belong to, from family to country to the wider world. Which of them made you most of who you are, and what would you want to pass on to the next generation?

title: Four Ways to Live Together: The Week in One Page
why: Monday opened with Jonathan Haidt and his memorable Rider and the Elephant. Our intuitions decide first, and reason arrives afterwards to tidy up the explanation.
text:
Monday opened with Jonathan Haidt and his memorable Rider and the Elephant. Our intuitions decide first, and reason arrives afterwards to tidy up the explanation. He then lays out moral foundations, six distinct receptors (care, fairness, loyalty, authority, sanctity and liberty) through which different groups read the world. The upshot is a kind of compassion: because different sides attend to different receptors, their views can look strange to one another.

Tuesday asked whether a free society must tolerate those who would destroy it. Popper's answer, in his 1945 book The Open Society and Its Enemies, was far more restrained than the slogan suggests. He did not want to shut down intolerant ideas while they could still be answered with reason and kept in check; what he wanted to refuse was the movement that will not play by those rules. In postwar Germany the idea became law: rights used to fight the democratic order can be forfeited, and parties that seek to abolish it can be banned.

Wednesday brought Steven Pinker's long arc. Violence, he argues, has declined across the long run of history, and the title comes from Abraham Lincoln's phrase for the better angels of our nature: empathy, self-control, the moral sense and reason. The change did not come from human nature itself but from institutions, the state, commerce, the growing respect for women's values, cosmopolitanism, and the escalator of reason that reframes violence as a problem to be solved. His clearest example is the tenfold to fiftyfold decline in European homicide rates since the late Middle Ages, and he keeps the book honest by noting that the decline was uneven, incomplete and not guaranteed.

Thursday closed with William James and the man walking round a squirrel in the mountains, while the whole camping party squabbled over the metaphysics of it. James's answer was to ask what practical difference the question made to your life, and the quarrel dissolved. That is the pragmatic method, primarily a way of settling disputes that otherwise might be interminable, and it extends its generosity even to grand idealist systems. A new truth, he says, grows much as a tree grows, grafting itself on to the ancient body of what we already believe. What ran through the week was a shared trust in reason as a bridge between people rather than a weapon. Haidt shows where our intuitions divide us and what each side misses. Popper shows how to defend tolerance without becoming intolerant. Pinker shows that the long decline of violence is the work of institutions and habits that can be maintained or lost. James shows how a quarrel can be dissolved by asking what it practically amounts to. Each edition was a different answer to the same question, how do people who see the world differently live together? The most inspiring moments were Pinker's humility, a book about progress that refuses to promise it, and James's squirrel, which turned a quarrel into a curiosity. The essayist Lee Harris, whose work anchors this series, saw ideology as a stage that people dress up in rather than a strategy to be followed through. This week's four thinkers offer a friendlier version of that diagnosis: Haidt names it moral intuition, and James shows that most intractable disputes dissolve once you ask what they practically amount to. Together they suggest that what Harris called fantasy is less the enemy than the material we work with, and the question is less whether to expose it than how to help people see past it. This week kept returning to one idea: that disagreement is not the same as enmity. Over the days ahead, when someone you care about feels strongly about something you do not, try one of the week's tools. Ask what practical difference the dispute would make to your life, or which moral foundations might be doing the work in each of you, and see whether a door opens where there was only a wall.

title: The Man Who Went Round the Squirrel
book: Pragmatism, Lecture II: What Pragmatism Means
author: William James
why: It begins with a scene. Some years earlier, James writes, he was with a camping party in the mountains and returned from a solitary ramble to find everyone 'engaged in a ferocious metaphysical dispute'.
text:
It begins with a scene. Some years earlier, James writes, he was with a camping party in the mountains and returned from a solitary ramble to find everyone 'engaged in a ferocious metaphysical dispute'. A man is pacing round a tree, and a squirrel on the tree keeps turning, so the trunk always stays between them. Does the man go round the squirrel? Everyone has taken sides, the numbers are even, and both sides appeal to James to make a majority. His answer is not a verdict. It is a distinction. The answer, he says, 'depends on what you practically mean' by the words: if you mean passing from the north of the squirrel to the east, then the south, then the west, the man obviously goes round; but if you mean being first in front of him, then on his right, then behind him, then on his left, the man fails to go round, because the squirrel keeps its belly turned towards him all the while. 'You are both right and both wrong', he concludes, according as you conceive the verb in one practical fashion or the other.

That little anecdote is the whole method, and it is a charming one. James calls it the pragmatic method, 'primarily a method of settling metaphysical disputes that otherwise might be interminable'. Take any idea and ask what difference would it practically make to anyone if this notion rather than that notion were true. If no practical difference whatever can be traced, 'then the alternatives mean practically the same thing, and all dispute is idle'. He says the term is derived from the Greek word pragma, meaning action, from which 'practice' and 'practical' come, and traces the principle to the American logician Charles Peirce, who in 1878 pointed out that our beliefs are really rules for action, and that to develop a thought's meaning we need only determine 'what conduct it is fitted to produce'.

Here James moves on to the theory of truth, 'the very central point' of the doctrine. Truth, he says, is 'one species of good', and 'the true is the name of whatever proves itself to be good in the way of belief, and good, too, for definite, assignable reasons'. Yet he is generous even to grand systems. Believers in the Absolute of idealism, he allows, have 'a right ever and anon to take a moral holiday, to let the world wag in its own way'. And he knows that beliefs guard one another: 'the greatest enemy of any one of our truths may be the rest of our truths'. A new truth, he says, grows much as a tree grows, grafting itself on to the ancient body of what we already believe. Pragmatism, in his words, is a 'mediator and reconciler' that 'unstiffens our theories'. Lee Harris spent his career applying this same method to politics. When he defined civilisation in Civilization and Its Enemies, he refused to make it an abstraction and instead described what a civilised society does in concrete life: it tolerates, it cooperates, it lessens its reliance on violence, and it keeps its gains across generations. That is James's pragmatic method carried into the life of peoples: we judge a way of living by its fruits, not by its principles on paper. It is still a useful habit today, because so many public arguments, and many private ones, are fought over words no one can actually point to. If you cannot say what would be different, you may be arguing about the label rather than about the world. James sketches the idealist's temper in this very lecture, and it deserves a moment. The rationalist, he writes, is 'comfortable only in the presence of abstractions', and for the rationalist truth is 'an absolute correspondence of our thoughts with an equally absolute reality', what we ought to think unconditionally. That demand is a real protection against drift, because if anything that works is true, so is any convenient fable. The two temperaments form a quiet pair: the pragmatist asks what an idea does in the world, and the idealist asks what it must be to deserve our belief, and each catches the other whenever it strays. The next time you find yourself in a quarrel that seems to have no end, try the man and the squirrel. Ask yourself what practical difference it would make to your life if one side were right rather than the other, and see whether the dispute is really about anything at all.

If you cannot say what would be different, you may be arguing about the label rather than about the world. James sketches the idealist's temper in this very lecture, and it deserves a moment. The rationalist, he writes, is 'comfortable only in the presence of abstractions', and for the rationalist truth is 'an absolute correspondence of our thoughts with an equally absolute reality', what we ought to think unconditionally. That demand is a real protection against drift, because if anything that works is true, so is any convenient fable. The two temperaments form a quiet pair: the pragmatist asks what an idea does in the world, and the idealist asks what it must be to deserve our belief, and each catches the other whenever it strays. The next time you find yourself in a quarrel that seems to have no end, try the man and the squirrel. Ask yourself what practical difference it would make to your life if one side were right rather than the other, and see whether the dispute is really about anything at all.

title: The Long Arc Towards a Gentler World
book: The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined
author: Steven Pinker
why: Steven Pinker's 2011 book opens with a claim that sounds like good news: violence in the world has declined on both the short and the long time scales, and the present is probably the most peaceful period in the history of the human species.
text:
Steven Pinker's 2011 book opens with a claim that sounds like good news: violence in the world has declined on both the short and the long time scales, and the present is probably the most peaceful period in the history of the human species. He supports it with a great deal of data covering military conflict, homicide, genocide, torture, criminal justice and even the treatment of children. The title comes from the ending of Abraham Lincoln's first inaugural address, and Pinker uses the phrase as a metaphor for four motivations in us that "orient us away from violence and towards cooperation and altruism": empathy, self-control, the moral sense and reason.

His more interesting claim is about where the change came from. It is not, he argues, that human nature changed in any biological sense, but that the cultural and material world shifted in ways that give our peaceable motives the upper hand. He names five historical forces. The Leviathan: the modern state and courts, "with a monopoly on the legitimate use of force", which break the cycle of revenge. Commerce: the exchange of goods and services, which means that "other people become more valuable alive than dead". Feminization: the growing respect for the interests and values of women. Cosmopolitanism: literacy, mobility and mass media, which expand the circle of sympathy. And the "Escalator of Reason", a metaphor he credits to Peter Singer, which reframes "violence as a problem to be solved rather than a contest to be won". His clearest example is the civilizing process: between the late Middle Ages and the twentieth century, European countries saw a tenfold-to-fiftyfold decline in their rates of homicide.

What keeps the book honest is its humility. Pinker reminds us that "The decline, to be sure, has not been smooth; it has not brought violence down to zero; and it is not guaranteed to continue." He also notes the paradox that our impression of violence has not tracked this decline, perhaps because increased communication makes every incident visible. Progress, in his telling, is not a property of the species. It is the product of institutions and habits that can be maintained, or lost. Several big names stand behind the argument: Thomas Hobbes, whose idea of the state as protector against the violence of everyone against everyone roots the Leviathan; the sociologist Norbert Elias, who first described the civilizing process; and the historian Lynn Hunt, who named the Humanitarian Revolution and its first organized movements to abolish slavery, dueling, judicial torture and sadistic punishment. The book is worth carrying today for its method as much as its optimism: it turns a comforting intuition into evidence, and shows that the peace we enjoy is the product of specific, nameable forces that can be studied, defended and extended. Lee Harris, for his part, looked at the same world through a lens of fragility. His essays on the enemies of civilisation and on fantasy ideology concentrate on the threats from within: demagoguery, tribalism and shared belief systems that, as Pinker puts of the fifth of his inner demons, justify unlimited violence in the pursuit of unlimited good. Harris is the watchman, Pinker the historian. Harris asks what threatens civilisation; Pinker shows how far it has already come, while conceding that it is not guaranteed to continue. Together they sketch a complete picture: reasons for an evidence-based hope, and reasons for keeping a careful watch. Look back over the past few weeks. Where did you see one of the better angels at work, in yourself or around you? What habit, institution or small act of reason made that moment possible?

title: The Kindness That Defends Itself: Popper's Paradox
author: Karl Popper
why: The paradox of tolerance is a question the philosopher Karl Popper named in his 1945 book The Open Society and Its Enemies. If a free society is genuinely tolerant, must it tolerate those who are not?
text:
The paradox of tolerance is a question the philosopher Karl Popper named in his 1945 book The Open Society and Its Enemies. If a free society is genuinely tolerant, must it tolerate those who are not? Popper's answer, in one memorable line, is that unlimited tolerance must lead to the disappearance of tolerance. A society that tolerates the intolerant without limit is, he warns, a society that will eventually be destroyed, and tolerance with it.

But Popper is careful, and his answer is far more restrained than the slogan suggests. He does not think intolerant ideas should be shut down at once. As long as they can be answered with reason and kept in check by public opinion, he writes, suppression would certainly be most unwise. The danger is the movement that will not play by those rules: it may begin by denouncing all argument and forbid its followers to listen to it. For such a movement, he argues, we should claim, in the name of tolerance, the right not to tolerate the intolerant.

In Germany this idea became law after the war. The country's constitution embodies what is called defensive democracy: if fundamental rights such as free speech or the right to assemble are used to fight the democratic order, they can be forfeited, and political parties that seek to abolish it can be banned. It is one of the clearest places where a democracy has written its answer to Popper's paradox into its own founding rules. The paradox grew out of an older conversation. Plato had noticed a similar knot, arguing that unlimited freedom would make the bully free to enslave the meek, and proposing as the fix a wise ruler rather than the messy rule of the people. Popper answered with something braver: the institutions of liberal democracy, free to criticise and correct themselves, are how a society defends its own openness. More than eighty years on, the same question keeps appearing, in debates over what social platforms may take down, in European constitutions, and in any community that wants to stay open to ideas without being swallowed by the worst of them. It sits neatly beside Lee Harris's thought on civilisation and its enemies: the open society is the one that learns to defend its openness without closing it. John Rawls saw the same question from the other end in A Theory of Justice (1971). A just society, he argued, must tolerate the intolerant, because a society that refused tolerance would itself be intolerant, and therefore unjust. He conceded, though, that if a society's security and the institutions of liberty were genuinely in danger, it could act in self-preservation. Starting from justice rather than from survival, Rawls lands very close to Popper's line, which is one of the things that makes the paradox so enduring. Where in your own life do you keep a door open to people or ideas you disagree with, and how do you keep that door from being forced shut from the inside?

title: The Elephant and the Rider: Why Good People Divide
book: The Righteous Mind: Why Good People are Divided by Politics and Religion
author: Jonathan Haidt
why: Haidt's first and most surprising claim is that our beliefs are driven primarily by intuition, with reason operating mostly to justify what we already feel.
text:
Haidt's first and most surprising claim is that our beliefs are driven primarily by intuition, with reason operating mostly to justify what we already feel. He calls this social intuitionism, and tells it with a memorable metaphor, the "Rider and the Elephant". The elephant is the vast, unconscious mind that in fact determines the direction, while the rider is the rational mind that thinks it is in charge and then works up explanations for decisions it never made. He is in good company: he points to David Hume and the biologist E. O. Wilson as thinkers who gave reason a "relatively low estimation", in contrast with Lawrence Kohlberg and his stages of moral reasoning, which put reason at the centre.

In the second part he lays out moral foundations theory: just as a tongue is organised to respond to different sorts of food, the human brain is organised to respond to several distinct kinds of moral violation. Haidt identifies six, the care or harm, the fairness or cheating, the loyalty or betrayal, the authority or subversion, the sanctity or degradation, and the liberty or oppression. In an interview he summed it up by saying morality "is at least six things, and probably a lot more than that". The practical upshot is a kind of compassion: because Republicans and Democrats tend to focus on different moral receptors, their views can look strange to one another, and Haidt says this leads to worse political tactics and worse decision making.

In the last part he introduces a hypothetical "hive switch", a capacity that turns a selfish human "chimp" into a "groupish" human "bee". Cultures and organisations, he notes, have techniques for making people identify with their groups, such as dancing, moving, and singing in unison. And there is a warmly personal note in the book: Haidt has been a liberal all his life, and working on these questions he has become more open to other points of view. Haidt is not alone in questioning the power of reason. Lee Harris, whom you have been reading, wrote The Suicide of Reason over the same suspicion, that civilisation runs on far more than logic. Where Harris keeps a wary eye on the ways group myth and ideology can turn against the civilisation that raised them, Haidt's aim is understanding and common ground. Both say something similar: if you want to know why people believe what they believe, you start with the feelings and the group, not with the arguments. Émile Durkheim, one of the founders of sociology, spent much of his career asking what creates the "we" in a society. He argued that it is shared rituals and collective experience that forge the solidarity which holds people together. Haidt's hive switch, with its dancing, moving, and singing in unison, is close to a modern restatement of Durkheim's insight that the group is born in the moments when people do something together. Where Harris keeps a wary eye on the power of the group, Durkheim and Haidt see the group as the soil in which community grows. Next time you feel very certain about something, notice whether it is your reasoning that speaks first, or your feelings. If your own moral foundations are doing some of the work, what might you be willing to ask of the people who feel just as strongly from a different place?

title: The Bonds That Hold Us: A Week in One Page
why: Monday opened with Lee Harris and his favourite trick: pressing something strange into a familiar shape.
text:
Monday opened with Lee Harris and his favourite trick: pressing something strange into a familiar shape. He begins with Montezuma, who had no category for the Spanish and so read them as the returning god Quetzalcoatl, a mismatch that proved fatal. Harris turns the same question on 9/11 and names what he calls a fantasy ideology: a belief that works like a stage, where the believer plays the hero of a cause he already accepts and treats everyone else as a prop. The example that stayed with me is Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, a war with no economic or strategic prize, demanded by the fantasy itself rather than serving any real end.

Tuesday met a very different voice in Carl Schmitt, the German legal theorist. His claim is blunt: the specifically political distinction is the one between friend and enemy. What keeps it alive is that the enemy is a role, not a name. Language, ethnicity, culture or religion turns political the moment a group uses it to define itself and becomes willing to defend that identity by force, and because each group decides for itself what counts as a threat, no outside judge can settle a truly political conflict.

Wednesday went back to the fourteenth century and a Tunisian scholar, Ibn Khaldun, who had already given social cohesion a name: asabiyyah, which his translator Franz Rosenthal rendered as "group feeling." It is the shared bond that lets a tribe defend itself and act as one. His bold claim is that this bond is cyclical: strongest at the birth of a civilisation, under the pressure of nomadic life, then thinning out as a dynasty grows settled and comfortable, and at last loosening into faction until a newer group with a fresher bond rises from the periphery.

Thursday brought in Karl Popper as a counterpoint. He names the story that historicists tell, that history obeys discoverable laws and so the future is already written, and traces it back to the doctrine of a chosen people, its two great modern faces being racialism and Marxism. His answer is the open society, a society whose first duty is the freedom of its citizens, where problems are fixed one by one in what he calls piecemeal social engineering, because if the future is genuinely open, the whole weight of responsibility falls back on us.

Friday closed the week back with Harris, in a short interview where he was careful with his word. He chose "civilisation" because it is value-free, describing a state of social organisation marked by tolerance, cooperation, a lessening reliance on violence, and above all stability. What struck me is that he calls it a transgenerational project, a trust that reaches across generations, and his clearest example is the Soviet Union, where when the state stopped being willing to apply terror, there was, in his words, "nothing there to hold them together." The week kept circling one question: what makes a group a group, and what keeps it together? Each thinker answered from a different end. Harris showed us the bonds that are staged rather than real, a fantasy that treats people as props. Schmitt gave us the raw minimum, a group defined by its willingness to fight alongside friends and against enemies. Ibn Khaldun named the bond itself, asabiyyah, and the quiet way that comfort wears it down. Popper warned against the story that pre-writes the future, because a society that believes its destiny is fixed quietly stops taking responsibility for the present. And Harris, in his closing interview, landed on the plainest version of all: civilisation as a transgenerational trust, the quiet glue of tolerance, cooperation and stability that you pass on.

What was most inspiring, honestly, was Ibn Khaldun. Fourteenth century, Tunisia, and he still saw that the very comfort a civilisation builds for itself is what slowly loosens the ties that hold it, and that the inheritance belongs to the people who still feel that bond most strongly. It is a sober and rather beautiful observation, and the one I kept returning to as I pulled the week together. Aristotle would have put the question differently, and it is a useful nudge. For him the real question was never just what holds the group together but what the group is for. In the Politics, the city is not merely a way of keeping people from perishing but a way of living well, and a life aimed only at survival is a diminished one. It sits comfortably alongside the week rather than against it: the bond matters, and it matters most when it is in the service of something worth living for. Here is the one question to take into the evening. Think of the group you most feel you belong to, the family, the team, the neighbourhood. What is the bond that actually holds it together, the shared history, the mutual trust, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it? If it were suddenly asked to hold a heavier weight than it was built for, what would you do to help it hold? There is no right answer. You only have to notice the bond, and decide what you would do to keep it strong.

title: What Holds a Society Together: Lee Harris in Ten Minutes
book: Our new epoch in history: 10 minutes with philosopher/political thinker/novelist Lee Harris
author: Bill Steigerwald (interviewing Lee Harris)
why: Harris starts by being careful with his word. He chose "civilization" because it is value-free, not a banner for us against them.
text:
Harris starts by being careful with his word. He chose "civilization" because it is value-free, not a banner for us against them. He defines it as a state of social organization marked by tolerance, by cooperation, by a lessening reliance on violence as a way of getting things done, and, most importantly, by stability. It is a picture of a society that has grown calmer rather than louder.

What strikes you is that he calls it a transgenerational project. A civilisation is not a snapshot; it is something you pass on. The values of your grandchildren should more or less reflect your own, and you hope they will not fall below the ethical baseline you set. There is real warmth in that: civilisation is trust that reaches across generations.

His best example comes from the collapse of the Soviet Union. The only reason to obey the orders there, he says, was fear of terror. When the state stopped being willing to apply terror, "there was nothing there to hold them together." The lesson he lands on is that a society has to have the ability to control its people in order to survive, and that the glue is far more fragile than most people assume. This is the quiet centre of Harris's whole project, the question of how a liberal society comes into existence and keeps existing. He gently pushes back on the assumption that when people get together, the first thing they do is construct a nice little society. That idea, civilisation as a deliberate and hard-won achievement that must be renewed by each generation, lands him in the company of the older thinkers who saw social order as something built rather than inherited. It is a sober and hopeful note for anyone who feels trust and shared institutions running thin: cohesion is a thing you make, not a thing you are born into. Ibn Khaldun saw something similar from the other end. The fourteenth-century historian wrote about asabiyyah, the social solidarity that binds a group together, and watched groups rise when that bond was strong and falter when it loosened. Both Harris and Ibn Khaldun are pointing at the same quiet fact: a society is only as durable as the bonds that hold it. Harris helps us see what a civilisation is; Ibn Khaldun helps us see how those bonds come and go. Look at the ties that hold your own community, workplace or circle of friends together. What shared habits, values or trusts make it more than a collection of strangers, and how do you notice when those bonds are quietly wearing thin?

title: The Future Is Not Written: Popper's Open Society
book: The Open Society and Its Enemies
author: Karl Popper
why: Today's reading is Karl Popper's defence of the open society, and it is a natural counterpoint to Lee Harris, because the two are working on the same ground: what happens when a people organise their lives around a story they believe is already written.
text:
Today's reading is Karl Popper's defence of the open society, and it is a natural counterpoint to Lee Harris, because the two are working on the same ground: what happens when a people organise their lives around a story they believe is already written. Popper gives that story a name and a method. He calls it historicism, 'the doctrine that history is controlled by specific historical or evolutionary laws whose discovery would enable us to prophesy the destiny of man.' The historicist believes the future has already been written, that if we can only read the laws of history we will know where everything is going. And that, Popper argues, is where the most dangerous ideologies come from: they promise a destination and then spend the present in the service of arriving there.

He traces the idea back to its oldest roots. In the first volume he argues that historicism grew 'out of the tribal form of social life', beginning with the doctrine of a chosen people whose destiny was fixed by God, and he finds its two great modern versions in racialism on the right and Marxism on the left. Both, he says, use the same method: an interpretation of history that claims to have found its law, and therefore to have a right to direct the present. That is a remarkable move, and worth sitting with. The promise of a guaranteed future is what makes these ideas so seductive, because it relieves us of a heavier burden: the open, unwritten, for all we know, possibility of what we might do next.

His answer is the one that gives the book its title. Popper calls it the open society: a society organised so that the protection of the citizens' freedom is the state's first duty, and where problems are fixed one by one rather than swept away in a single revolutionary act. He names this piecemeal social engineering, the practice of 'searching for, and fighting against, the greatest and most urgent evils of society, rather than searching for, and fighting for, its greatest ultimate good.' The quietly radical point is that the future is genuinely open. There is no law telling us what must happen. And if that is true, the whole weight of responsibility falls back on us, on the institutions we build and the arguments we are willing to test in public. Lee Harris spends his books naming the myths that organise our lives: the ideologies, the chosen narratives, the stories that make certain things unthinkable and certain acts inevitable. Popper, writing in the middle of a world war, identifies the same mechanism from the methodological side. For Harris the danger is that ideology turns people into characters in a fantasy. For Popper the danger is that historicism turns history into a prophecy. Both are myths, both mobilise, and both treat the present as a means to an imagined end. What each adds to the other is the answer. Harris helps us see the psychology and the culture; Popper helps us see the institutions. Between the two, we can tell where a myth is operating and how a free society might hold it at bay, by keeping the future open and by letting every argument be checked, criticised, and corrected before it is made law. It is worth knowing who Popper's first enemy is, because he places him in Athens rather than in a modern party. He reads Plato as the founder of the great historicist project. Confronted with the disorder of change, Plato's answer was to arrest it: to build a fixed state, run by philosopher kings, where the individual exists to serve the whole. Popper is generous where he can be. He praises Plato's analysis of social change even as he rejects his remedy, and he calls the generation of Athens before the Peloponnesian War the 'Great Generation', the moment critical discussion was invented and the open society first became possible. Plato and Popper, in other words, faced the same tremor in the ground: the fear that change leads to decay. Plato wanted to stop it. Popper wanted to build institutions that could keep going through it, one correction at a time. Read together, the two make the stakes clear. If the future really is not written by any law or destiny, what does that ask of the people and the problems in front of you this week? Which small thing, in your own corner, would you be willing to improve, without waiting for a grander plan?

title: The Glue That Holds Civilisation Together: Ibn Khaldun's Asabiyyah
author: Ibn Khaldun
why: Long before the phrase 'social cohesion' entered English political vocabulary, an Arab scholar in fourteenth century Tunisia had already given it a name.
text:
Long before the phrase 'social cohesion' entered English political vocabulary, an Arab scholar in fourteenth century Tunisia had already given it a name. Ibn Khaldun, writing his great work the Muqaddimah in 1377, called it asabiyyah, a word that in Arabic simply means 'group cohesiveness'. In the nomadic world he knew from experience, it was the bond that made a tribe able to defend itself, to share its burdens, and to act as one. When his translator Franz Rosenthal rendered the term into English, he chose the apt phrase 'group feeling', and it captures what Ibn Khaldun meant: that shared sense of belonging and purpose that makes people stick together not because they are forced to, but because they feel they belong to one another.

Ibn Khaldun made a bold claim that this bond is not static but cyclical. It is strongest at the very beginning of a civilisation, when a people is still shaped by the hard demands of nomadic life and the loyalty that comes with it. As a dynasty settles, becomes wealthy and comfortable, that group feeling slowly thins out. The rulers, far from the pressures that forged them, grow lax, their coordination weakens, and the shared bond 'dissolves into factionalism and individualism'. Eventually, says Ibn Khaldun, a new group with a fresher, stronger asabiyyah will rise from the periphery and take their place. He even offered a rough rule of thumb: no dynasty generally lasts more than three generations, roughly forty years each, because the bond that made it is not handed down intact.

What makes the idea memorable is its honesty. Ibn Khaldun was not writing a flattering account. He was saying that the very comfort a civilisation builds for itself is the thing that slowly loosens the social ties that held it together, and that the people who will inherit it will be the ones who still feel that bond most strongly. It is a sober and rather beautiful observation, and it has been read and argued over ever since. This connects to a question Lee Harris returned to again and again: what actually holds a society together, beyond law or economics or shared language? Tocqueville noticed a similar fragility in American society, and Durkheim gave the opposite condition, anomie, a name for the feeling of being untethered from the group. Ibn Khaldun's cycle, read generously, suggests that social cohesion is not a permanent feature of civilisation but something that must be renewed, generation by generation, or it quietly fades. Robert Putnam, writing in the 1990s, picked up the thread from a different end. His concept of social capital asked a more practical question: why do some communities trust each other and cooperate more easily than others? Where Ibn Khaldun described a natural cycle of rise and decay, Putnam was more interested in the institutions, habits and networks that can rebuild that trust within a society. The two perspectives complement each other: one describes the pattern, the other asks what can be done within it. Think about a group you belong to, a family, a community, a team, a generation of friends. What is the thing that actually binds it, the shared history, the mutual obligation, the quiet feeling that everyone is in it together? And what would happen if that bond were suddenly asked to hold a much heavier weight than it was built for?

title: Friend or Enemy: What Makes a People?
author: Carl Schmitt
why: Schmitt's central claim is memorable for its bluntness: "the specific political distinction … is that between friend and enemy." For him, the political is its own sphere, reducible to none of the others.
text:
Schmitt's central claim is memorable for its bluntness: "the specific political distinction … is that between friend and enemy." For him, the political is its own sphere, reducible to none of the others. Ethics sorts the good from the bad, the aesthetic the beautiful from the ugly, the economic the profitable from the unprofitable, but the political distinction belongs to none of these. Its measure is "the utmost degree of intensity … of an association or dissociation": on one side, the willingness to fight and die together with members of your own group; on the other, the willingness to kill simply because someone belongs to a hostile one.

What makes the idea durable is that the enemy is a role, not a name. The political is not tied to any particular marker. Language, ethnicity, culture, religion: any of them acquires political quality the moment a group uses it to define itself and becomes willing to defend that identity against others by force. If one distinction stops dividing people, another latches on and takes its place. And because each group decides for itself what counts as a threat to its way of life, a truly political conflict cannot be settled by an outside judge. It has to be lived through.

That last point carries the weight of his critique of liberalism. Schmitt thought the liberal hope, that all conflicts could be solved to everyone's advantage by civilisation, technology and amicable compromise, would leave life shallow and purposeless, and that a community no longer willing to draw a line between friends and enemies would wither in internal strife or be overwhelmed by one that still could. Schmitt drew on the line of thought running from Hobbes: a state is legitimate chiefly in so far as it can protect its members, and a state that can no longer name its enemies can no longer do that. Lee Harris made a cousin of the same move: his book Civilization and Its Enemies asks what happens when the ties that hold a civilisation together fray, and where its real enemies lie. Both thinkers are, in the end, diagnosticians. They want us to see that the groups we live in are real, that they have boundaries, and that the state of those boundaries decides more of our daily life than we like to admit. From the other end, the fourteenth-century Tunisian historian Ibn Khaldun saw the same dynamic. He argued that a group's social cohesion, the bond he called asabiyyah, is forged in opposition: communities rise when they are united against others, and decay when that bond relaxes. Where Schmitt was diagnosing how modern states think about themselves, Khaldun was describing how empires rise and fade over centuries. Read together, the two help us see that the enemy is not only a threat to a group, but part of what makes it. Think of a group you belong to, a neighbourhood, a workplace, a nation. Who or what do its members define themselves against? Does that answer feel natural, or a little unsettling?

title: A Stage, Not a Strategy: Harris on Fantasy Ideology
book: Al Qaeda's Fantasy Ideology: War without Clausewitz
author: Lee Harris
why: Harris opens with a story that belongs to no single nation or century. When the Spanish ships reached the coast of Mexico, Montezuma had no ready category for white men with steel and strange intentions.
text:
Harris opens with a story that belongs to no single nation or century. When the Spanish ships reached the coast of Mexico, Montezuma had no ready category for white men with steel and strange intentions. The only story his world offered was a myth, the return of the white god Quetzalcoatl, so that is what he expected, and the mismatch proved fatal. Harris's point is gentler than it first sounds: when an event is strange to us, we instinctively press it into our own familiar categories. The question he asks of the attacks of 9/11 is whether we were making exactly that mistake, reading a baffling act through the Clausewitzian idea that war is simply politics carried on by other means, a rational calculation with an end in view.

The essay's answer is a phrase of his own: a fantasy ideology. Harris first encounters it in a personal memory. In college in the late sixties, a friend planned to join a massively disruptive protest against the Vietnam War, and when Harris noted that it would likely backfire, the friend replied that it was, in his words, good for his soul. The demonstration was not about changing anyone's mind. It was a stage on which the protester played the hero of a cause he already believed in, and the commuters he lay down in front of existed only as props in the performance. Harris likens it to a game of Dungeons and Dragons played out in ideological symbols instead of medieval romances, and notes that the fantasist, in treating other people as props rather than as minds with wills of their own, is often surprisingly powerful.

The historical example that stays with you is the Italian conquest of Ethiopia. There was no economic or strategic gain to be had, and the diplomatic costs were severe. Ethiopia was a prop in the fantasy pageant of the new Italian Empire. The fantasy demanded that Italy conquer something, and the conquest was an end in itself rather than a means to one. Around it Harris gathers its siblings: the Jacobin dream of reviving the Roman Republic, Mussolini's Roman Empire, the antebellum South's sense of itself as the bearer of true civilisation, and, drawn from the French thinker Georges Sorel, the key insight Mussolini grasped. The Sorelian myth had to be presented as theater, with the audience's willing suspension of disbelief doing the work of persuasion. The essay stands quietly on a lineage worth knowing. William James asked what use a belief is when it cannot be scientifically demonstrated. The Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto extended that question to all the beliefs a society lives by. And the French thinker Georges Sorel, writing before the First World War, asked the further question of what happens when beliefs are deliberately manufactured, planted like seeds rather than catalogued like plants. Harris's contribution is to see ideology not as a description of the world but as a staging of it, and to notice that the make-believe can come to be an end in itself. The same essay defends an unfashionable word, the term evildoers, which he takes to strike exactly the right note. The lesson beneath it is the one worth carrying today: mistaking a symbolic drama for a rational strategy gets you all the wrong answers about what can be negotiated and what cannot. From a different quarter, Sigmund Freud looked at the same question from inside the group, asking what binds individuals to one another and to a leader. He found the answer in identification, a libidinal attachment he described as a kind of love. Harris shows the outside of the scene, the script and the props, while Freud shows the inside, the bond that keeps the audience in their seats. Together they suggest that a group's readiness to stop testing its story against reality has two faces, a play to perform and a tie to preserve. Is there a belief you hold, or a cause you once supported, that you would struggle to defend in a calm conversation? What do you think that belief was doing for you, describing the world, or staging it?
